concept.title: Shorthand properties
concept.shortdesc: A shorthand sets several related longhand properties in one declaration. The longhands are the properties that hold the individual values.

section.title: Shorthands set every sub-property
section.p: A shorthand sets all of its sub-properties, including properties whose values are omitted from the shorthand. Unless the shorthand’s definition says otherwise, each omitted sub-property receives its initial value.
For example, margin sets the four side margins:

One value sets all four sides. Two values set the top and bottom margins, then the right and left margins. Three values set top, horizontal sides and bottom. Four values set top, right, bottom and left, respectively.

Some shorthands also reset sub-properties that do not appear in their syntax. Such a sub-property is reset-only. For example, the border shorthand resets border-image properties even though its syntax cannot set their other values. Consult each shorthand’s property definition to see its full set of sub-properties and reset behavior.

section.title: Shorthand values and importance
section.p: The shorthand is expanded into its longhands at the location of its declaration. Those longhands then compete in the cascade like declarations written separately.
The margin shorthand comes later and sets margin-left to 1em. If a later declaration sets margin-left directly, that later longhand can win.

An invalid shorthand contributes no longhand declarations. If a shorthand is declared !important, its sub-properties are important too. A CSS-wide keyword used as the shorthand’s entire value applies to every sub-property, including reset-only sub-properties. A CSS-wide keyword cannot be combined with other shorthand values.

section.title: Resetting properties with all
section.p: CSS Cascade 5 §3.2, Resetting All Properties: the all property.
all is a shorthand that sets almost every property to one CSS-wide keyword. It excludes direction, unicode-bidi and custom properties.

This sets the included properties to their initial values. Use inherit, unset, revert or revert-layer to apply the corresponding CSS-wide behavior to those properties. See Inheritance and default values for the meaning of each keyword.

section.title: Shorthand definitions
section.p: Shorthands do not all use the same value order or number of values. Their property definitions specify the grammar, defaults for omitted values and reset-only sub-properties. The guides for backgrounds, fonts and other property groups describe the shorthands in those groups.
